summary: Improves TCP's resistance to blind in-window attacks by off-path attackers who try to inject spoofed packets. Larger windows and longer-lived connections, such as BGP, make guessing more feasible. It is a Proposed Standard.

eli5.summary: Closing a hole where an unseen attacker could butt into a conversation by guessing numbers.

subtitle: Small changes to how TCP checks incoming RST, SYN and data segments, so a blind attacker cannot easily tear down or corrupt a connection.

tldr.problem: An off-path attacker who guesses a connection's 4-tuple only has to land a spoofed RST, SYN or data segment anywhere inside the receive window, and larger windows and long-lived connections such as BGP make that practical.
tldr.mechanism: A reset is accepted only if its sequence number exactly matches the next expected one, any SYN in a synchronized state draws a challenge ACK, and ACK values must fall in a narrower range.
tldr.outcome: Blind attacks become much harder but not impossible. The RFC is a Proposed Standard and has since been updated by RFC 9293.

facts.label: Mean tries to inject a RST
Levels
facts.value: RST SHOULD, SYN SHOULD, DATA MAY

today: RFC 5961 is a Proposed Standard that has been updated by RFC 9293; read that RFC together with this one for the current TCP specification. The RFC itself says the changes make off-path attacks harder but do not stop on-path attacks.

sections.title: Why Blind In-Window Attacks Work
sections.content:
TCP has long been assumed safe from spoofed packets sent by an off-path attacker, because the attacker would have to guess the 4-tuple (source and destination addresses and ports) together with the 32-bit sequence number. The RFC says that assumption has weakened. Window sizes keep growing, and applications such as BGP keep connections up for a long time and tend to reuse predictable addresses and ports.

The key point is that the attacker does not need the exact sequence number. RFC 793 accepts a reset if its sequence number is anywhere in the receive window. The attacker guesses a starting number, then sends spoofed segments that step forward by the window size each time. The mean number of tries to inject a RST is 2^31 divided by the window size, not 2^31.

The RFC gives the arithmetic for two defaults: with a window of 32,768 an average of 65,536 packets is needed, and with 65,535 an average of 32,768. It calls an attack of that size feasible at today's access bandwidths.
sections.eli5: If a lock accepts any key that is close enough, a thief only needs a few tries. The bigger the window, the closer 'close enough' gets, so the easier the guessing.

sections.title: Who Should Apply the Fixes
sections.content:
The mitigations SHOULD be implemented in devices that regularly keep the kind of TCP connection most exposed to these attacks: long-lived ones whose endpoints can be determined, where no other anti-spoofing protection such as the TCP MD5 option can be used. In other cases they MAY be implemented.

The RFC notes that the TCP MD5 option makes these attacks effectively impossible for applications that can use it, such as BGP, but that some implementations may find it expensive. It also points to port randomization and initial sequence number randomization as ways to make off-path attacks harder, and refers to RFC 4953 for the wider set of defenses.
sections.eli5: Not every connection needs a bodyguard. The ones that stay open for a very long time, and whose address is easy to guess, need one the most.

sections.title: Stricter Handling of RST and SYN
sections.content:
For a RST in a synchronized state, the new rules say: if the sequence number is outside the receive window, silently drop it; if it exactly matches RCV.NXT, reset the connection (MUST); if it is inside the window but not an exact match, send a challenge ACK of the form <SEQ=SND.NXT><ACK=RCV.NXT><CTL=ACK>, drop the segment and stop processing it. In the SYN-SENT state a RST is still acceptable if its ACK field acknowledges the SYN.

A genuine peer that really did send the reset has no state left for the connection, so the challenge ACK makes it send a second RST. That RST takes its sequence number from the ACK, so it matches exactly and the connection is aborted. A spoofing attacker never sees the challenge ACK and cannot answer it.

For a SYN in a synchronized state, the rule is simpler: whatever the sequence number, TCP MUST send a challenge ACK and drop the SYN. A peer that really restarted answers with a RST and the connection is torn down, after which SYN retransmission re-establishes it. A spoofed SYN just produces an extra ACK that the real peer discards as a duplicate.

The RFC admits one corner case: if a restarted host reuses the same address and port and happens to pick an initial sequence number of exactly RCV.NXT - 1, the stale connection is not reset. It says this comes from RFC 793 itself, not from these new rules.
sections.eli5: If someone shouts 'stop!' from the crowd, you do not stop at once. You call back 'is that really you?' The real friend answers properly, and a stranger who cannot hear you gets nowhere.

sections.title: Blind Data Injection
sections.content:
An attacker can also try to slip data into a connection by guessing a sequence number inside the receive window. RFC 793 treats an ACK value as acceptable when it does not acknowledge data not yet sent, which in practice means a very wide range, so the attacker has to guess two ACK values per sequence guess. The RFC gives the mean number of tries as 2^32 divided by RCV.WND, which is twice as hard as the reset case.

If injected data lands in the reassembly queue, the result can be an ACK war or data corruption, and the RFC says the mitigation cannot prevent an ACK war once data has actually been injected.

The mitigation (MAY) adds one input check: an ACK is acceptable only if (SND.UNA - MAX.SND.WND) <= SEG.ACK <= SND.NXT, and other segments MUST be discarded with an ACK sent back. MAX.SND.WND is a new state variable holding the largest window the local sender has ever received from its peer. The RFC says this reduces but does not eliminate false segments, and that it also makes spoofed FIN segments harder.
sections.eli5: It is harder to sneak a fake page into a book if the librarian also checks that the page number fits a narrow range, not just any number.

sections.title: Recommendation Levels and ACK Throttling
sections.content:
The three mitigations carry different strength: RST is SHOULD, SYN is SHOULD and DATA is MAY. The RFC explains that data injection is perceived as twice as unlikely as the RST and SYN attacks, and that the choice of how many to implement is left to the implementer.

Because challenge ACKs can be triggered by spoofed segments, the RFC suggests ACK throttling. A system administrator configures how many challenge ACKs may be sent in an interval; its example is no more than 10 in any 5 second window. The time and count SHOULD be tunable, and the RFC says no timer is needed, since a timestamp and a counter are enough. An implementation SHOULD include such a mechanism as a fail-safe.

Smaller values favor protecting bandwidth and CPU. Higher values favor cleaning up stale connections faster.
sections.eli5: If a doorbell keeps ringing, you do not answer every single ring. You decide to answer only so many per minute so you do not get worn out.

sections.title: Compatibility and Middleboxes
sections.content:
The required mitigations are fully compatible with RFC 793 implementations, since they add no new assumptions. For the best effect both ends of a connection need the fix; a one-sided fix protects only that end.

A corner case can take more than one round trip to abort a connection, much like a lost original RST. The RFC then walks through three middlebox situations. A middlebox without the fix may resend a RST with an old sequence number, which could cause a RST/ACK war. One that computes RST sequence numbers at the high end of the window can behave similarly, and ACK throttling would limit it. Firewalls or NATs without the fix may drop the challenge ACK, leaving the end hosts with the connection open. The RFC says it is not aware of an implementation doing the second case, and that it is out of scope to mitigate badly behaved middleboxes.
sections.eli5: If a messenger in the middle garbles your questions, the conversation can get stuck. That is why both friends, and the people in between, should follow the same rules.

sections.title: Limits of the Protection
sections.content:
The RFC is explicit about what it does not do. The changes do NOT protect against on-path attackers and make off-path injection harder, not impossible. Fully protecting a connection against both on- and off-path attacks requires IPsec AH or ESP.

It also warns that forged ICMP messages give off-path attackers other ways to disrupt connections, and that unless spoofed ICMP is addressed (it cites RFC 5927), these mitigations may not give the intended level of protection.

Finally, the challenge ACK creates a reflector possibility: an off-path attacker can cause the victim to send an ACK for each spoofed RST or SYN inside its window. The RFC says this does not amplify, because the attacker must send one segment for each ACK the victim sends.
sections.eli5: A better lock keeps out strangers who cannot see your door, but it will not stop someone standing right next to you, so you may still need a stronger lock for that.
